1473.heavy: A heavy (H) syllable contains an historically long vowel or a rising diphthong. A light (L) syllable contains an historically short vowel.... There is no Weight-By-Position... closed syllables are not heavy. (Historic length is realized synchronically as vowel quality.)
1473.dflt: L L + final: penult by the stated iambic default ((LL)<S>, ex. (17) a.si.nI 'stone'), but a lexicalized subset takes antepenult ((18) u.ti.nAw); disyllables: penult; the source gives no all-light words long enough to test further leftward footing beyond L(LL)<S> -> penult (17dd a.ni.ku.chAsh).
1473.prule: One accent per word (pitch + intensity, not duration). Final syllable extrametrical and never accented (accent is penult or antepenult); quantity-sensitive at the nucleus only: heavy = historically long vowel or rising diphthong, closed syllables NOT heavy (no weight-by-position); iambic feet built from the right edge excluding the final syllable; End Rule Right. Net surface pattern: heavy penult -> penult accent; H L + final -> antepenult (regular, (13)), with a few lexical items showing penult (14); L L + final -> penult by the iambic default (17), but a sizeable lexicalized set has antepenult (18, 'moraic trochee'); disyllables -> penult regardless of weight; monosyllables accented. Abstract final endings (inanimate plural / obviative -h, reflex of lost short-vowel suffixes) count as the extrametrical syllable and force accent onto the (new) penult, giving apparent final accent (chi.man 'boat' vs chi.ma.nH 'boats').
1473.srule: None (one accent per word): 'Words have one main prominence or accent per citation form'; the authors posit further feet only as abstract constituents diagnosed by optional syncope/devoicing of short vowels in weak position, with no audible secondary prominence. Confirmed by Swain 2008 p. 37 ('no evidence of secondary stress'), Rose & Brittain 2011 p. 198 and Dyck, Power & Terry 2012 p. 122 ('only one pitch-accented vowel per word').

1474.dq: Basic word stress. In every word of more than one syllable, one of the syllables bears heavy stress ... (p.26) In addition to word stress, there are stress patterns in sentences as well, which often have the effect of shifting the heavy stress off a word that would ordinarily receive it. The negative particle [ná], for example, always carries heavy stress in the sentence.
1474.dloc: Ch. 2 'Pronunciation', sec. E 'Stress and Intonation', book pp. 24-26; dialect scope: Ch. 1 'Its dialects' pp. 6-7 and Ch. 2 intro p. 11
1474.heavy: Only a hedged native-word tendency: stress on the last syllable 'if the syllable ends in a consonant', else penult; no vowel-length criterion; authors subordinate it to 'not predictable'.
1474.dflt: n/a (tendency only: penult when the word is vowel-final)
1474.prule: Heavy (primary) word stress falls on one syllable per polysyllabic word but its location (final, penult, or earlier) is 'not predictable' and must be learned per word; a native-vocabulary tendency (final syllable if the word ends in a consonant, penult if it ends in a vowel) is stated and immediately rated as having as many exceptions as adherents; loans keep donor stress; stress-only minimal pairs exist (e.g. [áspa] 'mare' vs [aspá] 'spotted fever'); some affixes are inherently stressed.
1474.srule: Secondary stresses said to exist but unstudied; no placement rule given ('there seem to be secondary stresses in Pashto as well as primary stresses'; word-level patterns 'have not been studied to any great extent'); only impressionistic examples: [wə́daredəm] 'I stood' with [-ed-] heavier than final [-əm], [akhistúnkay] 'buyer' with the first syllable heavier than the second or fourth.

1474.idn: Source describes 'the central, or Kabul, dialect' (speakers 'live mostly in the Kabul, Logar, Ghazni and Parwan provinces'; Tegey & Robson 1996: 6, 11), distinguished there from the Kandahar (western) and Ningrahar (eastern) dialects and from 'the Waziri dialect' (p. 7); 'central' is the book's label, not Glottolog's…

morph.rootq: Basic rule is word-based, not root-based: 'The stress in native Pashto words is generally on the last syllable if the syllable ends in a consonant, and on the next-to-last (penultimate) syllable if the last syllable ends in a vowel ... The root is invoked only for stressed affixes: 'some affixes automatically carry heavy stress ... Many of those affixes always carry heavy stress: a word with one of these affixes will be pronounced with the stress on the affix rather than on the root of the word. For example, [-úna], one of the masculine plural markers, carries heavy stress'…
morph.elicq: 'The location of the heavy stress ... is not predictable in Pashto, and the spelling system does not mark stress at all. To ascertain where the heavy stress is in a Pashto word, the non-native speaker must ask a native speaker how to pronounce the word, and then listen for the stressed syllable.' (p.24-25); 'Stress patterns in polysyllabic words and in phrases and sentences have not been studied to any great extent ... (Studies of stress and pitch require extensive field work, and typically take place after more fundamental research on the language has been carried out.) It appears that in general, heavily stressed syllables are pronounced with higher pitch than weakly stressed syllables.'…

1475.dq: Stress refers to the relative prominence of a given syllable relative to other syllables in a word. ... Varma (1936: 92) further states that in “Lahnda” there is only one primary word stress; secondary word stress is not found.
1475.prule: Quantity-sensitive, unbounded, right-headed word stress in monomorphemic (root) words of Hazara Hindko (Haroon-Ur-Rashid 2015: a 6,000-word elicited corpus, the author a native speaker, plus a ten-speaker stress-marking test, sec. 5.4). Weight is three-way and moraic: light = CV with short /ɪ ə ʊ/ (1 mora; never word-final), heavy = CVV (long vowel or diphthong) or CVC (2 morae; codas moraic), superheavy = CVVC or CVCC (3 morae). (i) A superheavy syllable takes the stress wherever it stands (ˈkɑl.si.ri 'woman', tʃɑ.ˈbut̪.rɑ 'sitting place', sət̪.jɑ.ˈnɑs 'highly damaged', bə.ˈxɑr 'fever'); (ii) the final syllable is stressed only when it is superheavy (ɦɑ.ˈɽik 'seed'); (iii) otherwise -- syllables tied in weight, or all heavy -- the final mora is extrametrical and the penult is stressed (ˈsom.vɑr 'Monday', ˈbət.tɑ 'stone', ɦəd̪.ˈvɑ̃.nɑ̃ 'water-melon', fɑ.rɑ.ˈʃi.ʃi 'pear'); in sum 'The rightmost heaviest syllable is assigned stress' (p. 214). Bashir & Conners (2019: 49-50) state no placement rule for Abbottabad Hindko and defer ('For stress in Hindko we rely mainly on Bahri (1963), which... describes a Hindko variety different from that of Hazara'; Bahri's rule belongs to Awankari = sout2668): strong stress accent, one primary stress per word and no secondary stress (after Varma 1936), high-tone syllables always stressed, vowels flanking the stressed syllable shortened, stressed centralized vowels followed by geminates; their pair /ˈbaṭṭā/ 'stone' vs /baˈṭā-/ 'change, exchange' (p. 53) is consistent with (iii). Panjabi-type phonemic tone sits only on stressed syllables.
1475.srule: None: 'there is only one primary word stress; secondary word stress is not found' (Bashir & Conners 2019: 49, reporting Varma 1936: 92 on 'Lahnda'); confirmed first-hand for Hazara Hindko: 'Apparently, Hindko seems to have no secondary stress' (Haroon-Ur-Rashid 2015: 229).
1475.quote: Hindko is a quantity-sensitive unbounded rhythmic right headed language. Stress is taken by the super heavy syllable irrespective of its occurrence in words, otherwise penultimate syllable is assigned stress. In case of a tie in terms of syllable weight, extrametricality comes to play. [abstract p. iii] ... (a) Place the stress on the super heavy (tri-moraic) syllable, if available in the root ... (b) Stress the penult when there is a tie in syllable weight ... The rightmost heaviest syllable is assigned stress which may be bi-moraic or tri-moraic in a word. [sec. 5.3.3, pp. 211-214]
1475.loc: Abstract p. iii; sec. 5.3.3 pp. 211-214; sec. 5.4 p. 218
1475.idn: Haroon-Ur-Rashid 2015 (the cited rule): Hindko 'with a focus on its Hazara dialect' (Hazara Division: Haripur, Abbottabad and Mansehra districts, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan); data: the author is a native speaker; 'a corpus that contains 6000 Hindko words elicited in isolation and transcribed phonemically' (begun 2011) and ten speakers who 'come from Hazara Hindko dialectal region' (pp. 16, 39-40). Bashir & Conners 2019 (secondary stress, tone, affixes, clitics): the variety of Hindko spoken in Abbottabad; 'Elena Bashir conducted field work for four months in 2015 specifically working on data collection for the Hindko and Saraiki sections of the current work. During this time, she worked…
1475.tone: Phonemic tone of the Panjabi type (footnote 16: 'Tonal, or pitch accent, systems'): salient high-falling tone from non-initial voiced aspirates/h (/ánnā̃/ 'blind'; minimal pairs /baḍḍī/ 'large' vs /báḍḍī/ 'bribe', /dā/ 'of' vs /dā́/ 'ten'), weak low-rising tone with residual aspiration from initial voiced aspirates (/k(h)àr/ 'house'); 'In two-syllable words the high falling tone is always on the first syllable'. Tone is parasitic on stress, not a substitute for it: 'syllables uttered with high tone are always stressed (Bahri 1963: 191)' (p. 49); 'tone generally coincides with stress in Panjabi and Hindko: if a syllable is unstressed, it cannot carry a low tone, and usually does not carry a high tone' (p. 72). Hence the language is a stress language with a tonal contrast on the stressed syllable; Bashir & Conners give no stress-placement rule for this variety (Haroon-Ur-Rashid 2015, cited above, does).

morph.stmt: The grammar gives no one-line typological label, but every inflectional and nearly every derivational formative it describes for Hindko follows the root: nominal derivation is listed under 'Suffixal elements' (§4.2.1), case is layered after the stem ('Layer 1 consists of elements which attach directly to the stem; for these languages this means the oblique case. Layer 2 elements are added to the oblique case; the ablative and vocative cases, and simple postpositions, are such elements', §4.3.3 p. 96), and verbs are built as stem + participle/tense suffix + personal ending followed by auxiliaries…

1475.cfw: Haroon-Ur-Rashid (2015), the only first-hand study of stress in Hazara Hindko (a 6,000-word corpus and a ten-speaker test), gives a weight-sensitive rule (stress the superheavy syllable wherever it stands, otherwise the rightmost heaviest, and the penult when syllables tie) that nothing contradicts, while Bashir and Conners (2019) state no placement rule and rely for stress on Bahri (1963), who described a different Hindko variety, so the rule rests on a single source.

1477.dq: a template word-tone system: a system of culminative tone in which one lexical tone is assigned to a prosodic word.
1477.dloc: §1.5 pp.10-11 (typological summary: 'It is tonal.' p.10; 'template word-tone system... assigned to a prosodic word' top of p.11); Ch.3 'Tone and intonation' opener p.64; §3.1 p.65 incl. fn.97; §3.2 p.66; §3.3 pp.68-69 (four-syllable tonal template sentence is on p.69); §3.3.2 p.74 (alternating-verbs passage; only passing mention of 'stress')
1477.prule: No word-stress rule. Culminative 'word-tone' system: each prosodic word/tone group carries one lexical tone (H, F(alling), R(ising); some low/alternating verbs), realised on a four-syllable tonal template; tone of (usually) the left-most lexical element spreads rightwards, remaining syllables default low. Author explicitly follows Hyman (2011) in rejecting a pitch-accent/accentual analysis.

1478.prule: Default penultimate word stress ('generally'), but stress position is lexically specified and contrastive: an open class of polysyllabic words (historically schwa-penult cognates, plus Arabic/Dutch loans) carries final stress, six minimal pairs distinguished only by stress position are given ('angka 'lift up' vs ang'ka 'k.o. cake', 'barat 'west' vs ba'rat 'heavy', 'kiring vs ki'ring, 'pasang vs pa'sang, 'bolong vs bo'long, ba'gara vs baga'ra), and the author marks non-penultimate stress in phonemic transcription throughout the grammar.

1481.prule: Stress is phonemic (written in the transcription) and confined to the last two syllables of the stem: 'Primary stress always occurs on either the penultimate or ultimate syllable of a stem', with the choice lexical (e.g. 'lako, 'kaqan, 'lomba penult vs bo'ko, ke'dag, pos'qa final, all comparable shapes). No default position and no weight condition is stated for stem stress. The SIL orthography marks penultimate stress with an acute only where a word 'would otherwise be ambiguous', i.e. stress position distinguishes words. Suffix-triggered stress shift (authors: 'still tentative'): with -en/-an, stress shifts one syllable toward the suffix on all stem patterns except CVC'CVC with ultimate stress, where it stays (kog'kog -> kog'kogen, qak'yat -> qak'yaten), unless that stem is reduplicated C1eC2'C1eC2, which does shift (ket'ket -> ketke'ten). Reid 1971 entry 24 (Hettick 1966 inventory) lists 'Stress' as a phoneme after the segmental inventory: 'Consonants: p t k q [g] b d g m n ng s l w y Vowels: i ɨ o a Stress'.

1482.dq: Stress in Betsimisaraka can be understood as a bundle of co-occuring acoustic markers and segmental features that tend to occur on the penultimate syllable of morphological words, although several segmental interactions will result in surface stress falling on the final or antepenultimate syllable.
1482.dloc: Ch.5 'Stress and stress-assignment in Betsimisaraka', pp.114 (overview), 122-126 (sections 5.2-5.3, Tables 5.1-5.4, fnn.74-75), 130-131 (5.4 Conclusion)
1482.prule: Surface stress falls in a right-edge three-syllable window: penultimate is the usual case; antepenultimate is frequent but restricted to words whose final syllable has onset [k], [ʧ] or [ŋ] (very occasionally [n]) and whose last two vowels are identical (or final [a]) -- analysed as underlyingly consonant-final roots with an epenthetic final vowel invisible to stress; final stress occurs where hiatus resolution (coalescence /ai au/ -> [ε ɔ], diphthongization, deletion) has merged the last two underlying vowels (e.g. /mahai/ [ma'hε], /anau/ [a'nɔ]). No syllable-weight conditioning. Author's analysis: stress uniformly on the penultimate UNDERLYING vowel, with epenthesis and hiatus resolution ordered after stress assignment.
1482.srule: Secondary stress on alternating vowels leftward from the primary (penultimate underlying) vowel; outside compounds no two adjacent syllables are stressed (e.g. [ˌmandə'lovə]). In compounds each root is stressed separately and the first root's stress is secondary (ˌlava'k-oruŋu 'nostril'). Secondary stress is marked in the author's transcriptions only exceptionally.
1482.quote: The factors unified under the stress umbrella will be shown to occur almost entirely on the penultimate or antepenultimate syllables of words. The latter case will be seen to only occur only if the final syllable begins with one of [k, ʧ, ŋ], similar to the the “weak” syllables of OM. ... all antepenultimate stress is due to underlyingly consonant-final forms, which receive penultimate stress, but also an epenthetic vowel ignored by stress assignment. ... 1485.dq: Basically, the system is one of quantity sensitive iambic feet built from the left edge of the word (Valentine 1996:312); 'in the second part, word stress in Border Lakes Ojibwe is analyzed' (Swierzbin 2003:343).
1485.dloc: Valentine 1996 pp. 312-314, section 'STRESS' (and p. 288 on Fiero 1964 / Valentine 1987 for Berens River); Swierzbin 2003 p. 343 ('word stress... is analyzed'), p. 349 (weight), pp. 356-359 (patterns), p. 367 (Conclusion)
1485.heavy: Long vowel = heavy (iamb's weak position 'may only be filled by a short vowel', Valentine); Swierzbin: 'CVC syllables are light in Border Lakes Ojibwe and do not attract stress'; long-vowel syllables heavy (WSP 'Heavy syllables are stressed').
1485.dflt: All-short-vowel words: iambic alternation from the left, stress on every second syllable (2nd, 4th...); Swierzbin could not decide whether primary is on the 2nd or 4th in 6-light-syllable words, and some words show initial stress; Valentine reports 'stress shifts in sequences of short vowels' in northern Ontario dialects.
1485.prule: Quantity-sensitive iambic feet parsed left-to-right from the left edge of the word; the weak slot of a foot may hold only a short vowel, so every long vowel heads a foot and is stressed; final syllable often treated as extrametrical. For Berens River (Pikangikum) Ojibwe, a nort2961 dialect, Valentine states the same quantity-sensitive iambic pattern holds with pitch as the correlate. Valentine 1996 does NOT locate main (primary) stress for the northern dialects ('remains to be worked out'). Swierzbin 2003 (Seine River FN, Rainy River district doculect): primary stress on the rightmost non-final heavy (long-vowel) syllable; on the final syllable in HH disyllables; CVC is light.
1485.srule: Rhythmic (non-primary) stresses on the head of every quantity-sensitive iamb parsed left to right: each long-vowel syllable, and every second syllable in a run of short vowels ('stressed on every second syllable starting from the left'; in heavy+light words 'the heavy syllable has primary stress and every second syllable starting from the heavy syllable has secondary stress', with a four-syllable variant heavy = primary, final = secondary); no degenerate feet, so a leftover single light syllable is unstressed. Explicit in Swierzbin 2003 for Border Lakes (Seine River) Ojibwe; Valentine 1996 gives the same iterative iambic footing for Berens River (pitch alternations on stressed vs unstressed vowels) without separating primary from secondary.

morph.elicq: Jastrow 1980 §9.1.3.4 is a comparative handbook statement drawing on dialect monographs and the author's fieldwork; it gives no elicitation method. The only framing is diachronic-comparative: "Fast überall läßt sich die heutige Betonung auf die ältere quantitative Regel zurückführen ..."; forms are cited as isolated words with glosses, e.g. "(Mardin) ákəlna »unser Essen«, (Qarṭmīn) akə́lna", "Im Muslimisch-Bagdadischen kann man ḍúrbata und ḍurbáta »sie schlug ihn« hören". (Ahmed 2018:28 on Mosul merely restates Erwin's Iraqi-Arabic rule: "stress may lie on one of the last three syllables of a word, particularly on the syllable containing a long vowel".)
morph.stmt: No source gives a one-line typological profile; what they describe is Semitic root-and-pattern morphology (perfect/imperfect stems, geminate/ablaut causatives, templatic verbal nouns and broken plurals) combined with person SUFFIXES in the perfect and person PREFIXES (+ number suffixes) in the imperfect, pronominal object/possessor SUFFIXES, plural suffixes -īn/-āt(-ad), and a pre-verbal cluster of prefixed markers — Jastrow 1980:154: "Die große Mehrzahl der qəltu-Dialekte hat einen »present marker«, d. h. ein Morphem, das dem Imperfekt präfigiert wird... 1487.prule: No word-stress rule. Kashoki & Mann 1978 (statement over all Zambian Bantu languages, Nsenga enumerated among the Eastern Province languages): syllables 'more or less evenly stressed', stress 'does not distinguish words', every syllable carries tone (two contrastive tones, H and L), and in all Eastern Province languages the penultimate syllable of a word is automatically lengthened, and the slightly greater penult 'force' heard in some languages (e.g. Cewa) 'may be the effect of the lengthening of the vowel'. Simango 2006 (language-specific modern sketch): lexical and grammatical tone (H, L, Falling) and 'penultimate vowels are lengthened... not phonemic'; the words 'stress'/'accent' never occur. Ranger 1928 (missionary handbook, no tone analysis) calls the same penultimate prominence 'stress... laid on the penultimate syllable'; reconcilable as penultimate lengthening in a tone language.

1487.tone: Tone language. Kashoki & Mann 1978: 'A characteristic feature of ali Zambian languages is that each of their syllables carries tone... There are only tvvo contrastive tones in Zambian languages, high and low'; stress is non-distinctive and syllables are evenly stressed apart from the automatically lengthened penult. Simango 2006 sec. 2.1.2: 'two basic tones: High and Low... complemented by a Falling tone... used to index lexical as well as grammatical meaning', minimal pairs lini(Fall) 'not' vs lini 'when', mtanda(H) 'cross' vs mtanda 'lump of thick porridge', cenze(H) 'cicada' vs cenze 'it was'; grammatical tone on verbs (nikalye indicative vs subjunctive etc.); 'The distribution of tone in verbs and nouns is influenced by morphological... as well as syntactic factors' (mwana Falling vs mwana wangu all-H); cites Miti 2001 'A linguistic analysis of ciNsenga' and Miti 2002 (CASAS; Glottolog also lists Miti 2002 'Tone shifting in CiNsenga pronouns' and Miti 2003 on verbal tone; none reached). No stress or accent rule in either modern source; penultimate prominence = non-phonemic lengthening. Ranger 1928 calls it 'stress' and separately notes 'the meaning of a word hangs upon the intonation ofa syllable' (chitutu), an unanalysed hint at the tone contrasts.

The convention followed in marking tone for ciNsenga is to indicate High and Falling tone on the relevant vowels and to assume Low as the default tone (see also Miti 2001, 2002). Lexical functions of tone are shown in (4) and grammatical uses are shown in (5). (4) lîni 'not' lini 'when' mtánda 'cross' mtanda 'lump of thick porridge' cénze 'cicada' cenze 'it was' ...

1487.cfw: Nsenga is tonal by every modern source, but the record's other leg, no word stress, rests on one hedged survey sentence (Kashoki & Mann 1978, generalising over Zambian languages with Cewa as the example) and the silence of a 21-page sketch of one dialect (Simango 2006), while the most detailed Nsenga-specific description in hand, Ranger 1928, states a penultimate-stress system with alternating secondary stress and stress shift off object infixes; that is an old, non-specialist source and it loses, and Miti 2001 is only known second-hand, so this is a clear winner with few sources and a mild disagreement, not a clear consensus.

1488.tone: Gussenhoven 2006 (TAL; fuller version Phonology 23:193-223) analyses the prominence as an obligatory, culminative, 'metrically bound' accent realized solely by an H tone (default L elsewhere); deaccenting is neutralizing, so Nubi 'is not a typical stress-accent language' by Beckman's criterion, nor a tone language: 'a pivot between the classes of tone languages and stress-accent languages'. 1489.prule: Four-way lexical tone contrast (level, heavy, creaky, stop) on every full syllable; toneless 'weak' (schwa) syllables occur only prefixed to a toned syllable. No word-stress rule is given: 'stress' is mentioned only as a connected-speech factor 'affecting expressions, and perhaps clauses and sentences' (pitch lowering of the less important of two neighbouring syllables; particles often unstressed), and is explicitly left uninvestigated (App. C item 3).
1489.srule: Not mentioned in Okell 1969 (ch. 1 'Sounds' secs. 1.6-1.22 and App. C read): stress is named only as a connected-speech pitch effect 'not discussed in this Grammar'; no secondary or rhythmic stress is described. (Watkins 2001 p. 293 and Green 2005 p. 13 likewise give none: each tone-bearing major syllable is its own monosyllabic foot, schwa minor syllables unfooted.)

1489.tone: Okell: four tones (stop, creaky, heavy, level); the low-vs-high tone difference 'sometimes sounds like stress to English ears'; stress is a connected-speech/phrase-level pitch-lowering effect, 'not discussed in this Grammar', flagged in App. C as needing study ('the possibilities of stress (1.15 note)'). Weak (toneless schwa) syllables are always pretonic to a full syllable, i.e. the only word-internal prominence asymmetry is full-vs-reduced syllable, not a positional stress rule.

1490.heavy: a long syllable, i.e. one containing a long vowel ('unless the second syllable is long'; Kobès: 'une voyelle longue')
1490.prule: Word stress falls on the first syllable of the lexeme, unless the second syllable is long (contains a long vowel), in which case stress falls on that second syllable (Rialland & Robert 2001, after Sauvageot 1965, Njie 1982, Ka 1988/1994). Kobès 1869 states the same: initial 'accent tonique' in di- and trisyllables unless a later syllable has a long vowel.
1490.srule: Not mentioned in the cited works: Rialland & Robert 2001 give no secondary-stress placement (n. 14, p. 937, only suspects that 'allowance should be made for several degrees of stress' and leaves the question unstudied); Kobès 1869 is silent on secondary accent. A later work, Bell 2003 (WPCPL 15: 7-8, data from Ka 1988 and Hammond 1993), states that only heavy syllables, i.e. those with a long vowel, attract secondary stress (wax.táa.nu.kàay vs wo.yáa.na.ti; xáa.raa.nàat, fáay.daal.wàat) and that two adjacent syllables cannot both be stressed (wóo.waat).

evidence_works.detail: Typological survey; all Kinga data are taken from Schadeberg 1973 (no new first-hand material). It agrees with the entry's coding (kind = tonal, tone_cls = restricted-tone, one H per word, mora-counted) and adds the typological placement: Kinga is one of the 'analytically indeterminate' obligatory-one-H systems that could be read as restricted tone, pitch accent or stress-accent 'where stress would be realised simply as H pitch' (p. 228); by Hyman's definition (3) it is tonal because 'only pitch is involved' (p. 230); restricted-tone Kinga (with Bena) 'have kept the vowel-length opposition, and do not show evidence of penultimate stress' (p. 240); because Kinga assigns 'their obligatory /H/ by mora, their obligatory /H/ cannot be SA' (p. 242, ex. 18b lists Schadeberg's antepenultimate-H verb forms); Table II (p. 245) files Kinga as +obligatory, +culminative ('Words have exactly one H mora in Kinga'); p. 251 notes a reviewer's alternative cut under which 'Kinga and Safwa would have SA, despite the fact that they count moras rather than syllables', which Hyman does not adopt. 1494.dloc: Misnadin & Kirby 2018, section 'Word stress', pp. 121-122; Kiliaan 1897 sec. 111, pp. 83-84; Davies 2010 p. 51
1494.prule: No genuine word stress. Kiliaan 1897: accent has no fixed place (heard now on the penult, now on the final); strictly speaking Madurese has no real syllable stress, prominence on a syllable reflects the speaker's mood/emphasis (oratorical accent). Davies 2010: word stress not salient; intonation group is the lowest relevant phonological unit; isolated words show stress on almost any root syllable. Misnadin & Kirby 2018: no phonetic evidence of word stress, lexical or otherwise (impressionistically initial in 2-3-syllable words, antepenult in 4-syllable words).
1494.srule: Kiliaan 1897 sec. 115 only (within an account that denies fixed syllable stress): words of four or more syllables are pronounced in at least two parts, and each part can carry its own accent, so a secondary accent (bijaccent) is often distinguishable from the main accent, in either order (noroq-aghija: main on ghi, secondary on no, 'or the reverse'); tendency to accent the last syllable of the first part. Nothing on secondary stress in shorter words. Not mentioned in Misnadin & Kirby 2018 ('Word stress', pp. 121-122), Misnadin 2016 (sec. 2.3.4, pp. 51-52) or the Davies 2010:51 passage.

However, there is at present no phonetic evidence of word stress in Madurese, lexical or otherwise. ... 1495.prule: No contrastive stress; no tone or length contrast. Stress is hard to hear, often level across syllables, and the same word varies in stress placement across repetitions. Isolation bisyllables: first syllable often stronger but second carries rising pitch. In carrier frames all words (affixed or not) were final-stressed, with secondary stress on syllable 1 of 3-4-syllable words and syllable 2 of 5-syllable words (the two often equal). Author: analysis 'remains uncertain', stress 'not significant in Kwomtari phonology'.
1495.srule: In carrier frames (primary stress word-final), words of more than two syllables also showed secondary stress: on the first syllable of three- and four-syllable words and on the second syllable of five-syllable words; in five-syllable words the two stresses often sounded equal. Frame condition only; nothing stated for longer words; author calls the whole stress analysis 'uncertain'.

1497.prule: Stress is final in the ROOT, inside a strict two-syllable right-edge window, and is not computable from the word's syllable count: Geurtjens 1926:3-4 gives final stress only 'as a general rule', 'in no case' earlier than the penult, with penultimate stress in 'many derived words with suffixes' and 'a lot of proper names' (ST1 adds words ending in schwa and 'a few other words'); Drabbe 1955:16 (via Usher) restricts invariable final stress to roots 'as opposed to compounds and inflected forms' and calls stress 'sometimes contrastive due to inflection and compounding'; Olsson 2021:174 (via Wikipedia) puts the single stress of an inflected verb on the final syllable of the prefixal complex, not word-finally. 1498.tone: Two contrastive pitch levels (high, low) combine with stress: a stressed high-pitch syllable gets increased intensity (marked acute: íko, iré), a stressed low-pitch syllable gets length (marked grave: ikò, ìre). Both stress position and pitch level are lexically contrastive (four-way quadruplet on disyllables, p.474). Olson frames this as contrastive word-level STRESS, not tone; a pitch-accent reading (lexical accent position + H/L accent type) is possible but the source's term is stress. 1499.prule: One accent (high pitch, usually with greater loudness) per word on a lexically fixed vowel; its place is not predictable from the word-form and is contrastive (minimal pairs by accent place). Most verb-forms carry two accents (secondary on a root vowel, primary on a categoric morpheme's vowel, interchangeable); a few proclitic/enclitic 'sub-words' are accentless.
1499.srule: Non-verbal words have one accent only. Most verb-forms have two: a secondary accent (lower pitch) on a vowel of the root-morpheme and the primary on a vowel of a categoric morpheme (which morpheme is accented is specified per verbal category); the two may exchange rank when the lexical meaning is contrasted. Some proper names of more than two vowels have an optional secondary accent on a vowel preceding the primary (absent in fast speech); sámsám has two equal accents.

dfl.note: Anceaux states there is no rule fixing the place of the accent (minimal pairs kíe/kié, mére/meré, síe/sié, tébu/tebú, p. 37) and gives no majority position. May & May 1981 p. 10-11 add that placements are 'of two main types, ultimate and penultimate', antepenultimate in 'a relatively small number of words', with a closed-syllable tendency in non-verbal forms, otherwise 'no general rule governs stress placement. In this, our data supports Anceaux (p. 37).'
dfl.q: So in a word there usually is one vowel, and that always the same, which has the accent. However, there is no rule by which the place of the accent in all words is determined.
dfl.c: Anceaux 1965, The Nimboran Language: Phonology and Morphology (VKI 44)

vlen.q: In non-verbal forms the stress usually falls on a closed syllable where one occurs, although there are exceptions. Where there are no closed syllables, or more than one, no general rule governs stress placement. In this, our data supports Anceaux (p. 37).
vlen.c: May & May 1981, Nimboran phonology revisited (Irian 9(1): 9-32)

tn.quote: The accent is a quality of vowels and consists of a pitch, higher than that of the other vowel(s) of the same word, usually combined with a higher degree of loudness (stress). As this higher degree of loudness is not always heard, it apparently is less essential than the high pitch is, but the stress is observable in the majority of cases and therefore it must be mentioned here. ... Most words have one and only one accent; exceptions to this rule will be discussed separately below. ... However, there is no rule by which the place of the accent in all words is determined.
tn.cite: Anceaux, J. C. 1965. The Nimboran Language: Phonology and Morphology. Verhandelingen van het Koninklijk Instituut voor Taal-, Land- en Volkenkunde 44. 's-Gravenhage: Martinus Nijhoff.
tn.locator: pp. 36-37, Part One ch. VII 'The Accent', sec. 1 'Description of the accent'
tn.note: Word accent realised mainly as high pitch (loudness secondary), one per word, place lexical and contrastive (kíe 'hand' vs kié 'time'); verb-forms may carry two accents; no tone inventory given.
